St. Euphrosyne of Alexandria

Saints

St. Euphrosyne of Alexandria

Smaragdos · Smaragdus

Period
Fifth century in the received life
Region
Alexandria; Egyptian monastery
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Woman
Commemoration
September 25

Introduction

St. Euphrosyne’s received life concerns a woman who enters a men’s monastery under the name Smaragdos and remains unrecognized by her father. Her identity is disclosed near death, and Paphnutios subsequently becomes a monk.

Read the published life [1]

There was a man of Alexandria named Paphnutius, honourable, and observing the commandments of God.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

There was a man of Alexandria named Paphnutius, honourable, and observing the commandments of God. He married a wife worthy of his race, and of honest manners, but she was barren. Thereat the man was troubled much and sorrowful, likewise his wife was sore afflicted, seeing the distress of her husband. And after some time he told a certain abbot his desire; and he, compassionating him, besought the Lord to give him a child. Then God heard the prayers of these twain, and gave to Paphnutius a daughter. After that, Paphnutius brought his wife to the monastery, that she should be blessed by the abbot and the brethren. And when the little girl was seven years old, she was baptized, and called Euphrosyne, and her parents rejoiced over her, because they had received her of the Lord, and she was comely of face. Now when she was twelve years old, her mother died, and she lived with her father, who taught her her letters, and to read, and all the rest of the world’s knowledge. The good report of her spread through the town, for she was wise in knowledge, and very comely, and composed in face and spirit. Thus many desired to mate her with their sons, and tried to come to terms with the father, but could not gain their point; for he said, “God’s will be done.” But one man excelled all in wealth and honour, and he sought the father and asked him to give his daughter to his own son in marriage; and he consented; so the usual betrothal gifts were made.

Baring-Gould’s1914 retelling from the Lives of the Fathers,volII,February,printedp265. It is a later hagiographic narrative; the book’s February placement is not substituted for the Orthodox September25 commemoration.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolII,February11,printedp265,first complete biographical paragraph

Life and notable events

The OCA relates that, rather than accept the arranged marriage, she distributes her possessions, disguises herself and enters the monastery. It says she spends38years in a solitary cell, while her grieving father receives consolation from the person he does not recognize.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Departure, concealment and38years

Death and martyrdom

Before death she reveals her identity and asks that her father prepare her body. The source describes burial, not an execution or martyrdom.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Death and disclosure

… And on the third day he said, “I have waited, my brother!” Then Smaragdus knew that he should not survive that day, and he said to Paphnutius, “Draw near to me.” And he drew near. Then said Smaragdus, who is also Euphrosyne, “Because the Almighty Lord hath brought me to the end of my contest, not by might of mine, but by His help, there remaineth to me the crown. And now I would not have thee troubled about thy daughter—I am thy daughter, Euphrosyne, and thou art my father, Paphnutius. And now I pray thee, (for none know that I am a woman), when I am dead do thou, my father, wash and lay me out for my grave, and pray for me.” And when she had said this, she gave up her soul. …

Baring-Gould’s1914 retelling from the Lives of the Fathers,volII,February,printedp265. It is a later hagiographic narrative; the book’s February placement is not substituted for the Orthodox September25 commemoration.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolII,February11,printedp271,disclosure and death

Writings and legacy

After her burial, Paphnutios distributes his wealth and lives ten years in her cell. The OCA commemorates father and daughter on September 25 and again on February 15; the historical Western collection uses a different calendar placement.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Closing paragraphs and observances

    Her mother dies when St. Euphrosyne is twelve.

  3. End of life
